A leash is a long, narrow strap, cord, or chain that connects an animal — most often a dog — to a person, so the person can control where the animal goes.

Think of it this way: one end of the leash clips onto the animal's collar (the band around its neck), and the other end stays in the hand of the person walking it. This simple connection gives the person physical control over the animal's movement.

A leash is typically 1 to 2 metres long, though lengths vary. It is narrow enough to hold comfortably in one hand, and it usually has:

  • A metal clip or hook at one end, to attach to the animal's collar.
  • A loop or handle at the other end, for the person to hold or wrap around their wrist.

Leashes can be made from leather, nylon, rope, or chain — the material depends on the size and strength of the animal.

The leash restricts the animal's movement and keeps it close to the person holding it. Without a leash, a dog could run into the road, dash toward strangers, or simply disappear. The leash gives the holder direct, physical authority over the animal — if the dog tries to move in a direction you don't want, you pull back, and it stops.

This is why leashes are required in most public spaces like parks, streets, and shops. The rule exists to protect the animal, other people, and other animals.
The key idea behind the word

The central concept a leash carries is controlled restraint — allowing movement, but only within limits set by the one holding the leash. The animal is not immobile; it can still walk, sniff around, and explore — but always within the length of the leash, and always under the control of the holder.
Figurative meaning (when used about people, not animals)

The word "leash" is very commonly used in a figurative sense — meaning it moves away from its literal, physical meaning and is used to describe human situations involving control and freedom.

When we say someone is "on a leash," we mean they are being tightly controlled by someone else and do not have much freedom to act on their own. This is usually said with a slightly negative or critical tone, because it compares the person to an animal being controlled.

Common figurative expressions:

  • "On a leash" — under someone's control; not free to act independently.
  • "On a short leash" — under very tight control; given very little freedom or independence.
  • "Keep someone on a leash" — to make sure someone doesn't act too freely; to monitor and restrict their behaviour.
  • "Slip the leash" — to escape from someone's control; to get free.
  • "Off the leash" — free from control or restrictions; allowed to behave as one wants (often used when someone is finally free to act without supervision).

Literal use (about animals):

  1. She clipped the leash onto her dog's collar before stepping out for a morning walk.
  2. The notice at the park gate said: All dogs must be kept on a leash at all times.
  3. The puppy tugged so hard at the leash that it nearly pulled her off her feet.
  4. He dropped the leash for just a second, and the dog bolted across the garden.

Figurative use (about people):

  1. The new manager kept the whole team on a short leash — nobody could make a single decision without his approval.
  2. Now that she had left that controlling relationship, she finally felt off the leash.
  3. The government kept the press on a tight leash, making independent reporting nearly impossible.
  4. He had been on a leash his whole career; this new job was the first time anyone trusted him to work freely.

A leash is a strap or cord used to physically control an animal by connecting it to a person. Its core meaning is about restricting movement while maintaining connection and control. Figuratively, it describes any situation where a person's freedom and independence are limited by someone else's authority. The expressions built around the word — on a leash, off the leash, short leash — all extend this same idea of control, restriction, and freedom.
